content: Telogen effluvium is a condition characterized by sudden and widespread hair loss, which occurs due to a disruption in the normal hair growth cycle. This disruption is frequently triggered by a traumatic event, such as undergoing chemotherapy, experiencing childbirth, entering puberty, undergoing major surgery, enduring severe stress, or suffering from a severe chronic illness. These events cause a large number of hair follicles to simultaneously enter the telogen phase, which is the resting stage of the hair growth cycle. Approximately three months after entering the telogen phase, the hair follicles transition into the anagen phase, which is the active growth stage. During this process, new hair begins to form beneath the old hair, pushing the old hair out of the follicle. This results in a period of diffuse hair shedding. In most cases, telogen effluvium resolves on its own without the need for medical intervention and can affect individuals of any age. There is also a chronic form of telogen effluvium, which is similar in nature but persists over a longer period of time without resolving spontaneously. A common example of telogen effluvium occurs in women after pregnancy. During pregnancy, elevated estrogen levels provide a protective effect on hair, prolonging the growth phase. However, after delivery, when estrogen levels drop, this protective effect is removed. As a result, many women experience significant hair shedding a few months postpartum. This shedding typically resolves on its own, and hair regrowth usually begins within three months.
